subject: chemistry-hl
topicLabel: R1.4 Entropy and spontaneity (additional higher level)
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

items.topicLabel: R1.4 Entropy and spontaneity (additional higher level)
choices: The total heat energy stored in a substance
The dispersal of energy and matter, often seen as disorder
The rate at which a reaction proceeds
The energy needed to start a reaction
items.note: S measures how spread out energy and particles are. Gases > liquids > solids.

items.topicLabel: R1.4 Entropy and spontaneity (additional higher level)
items.stem: Which change has the largest increase in entropy?
choices: H₂O(s) at 200 K → H₂O(s) at 250 K
items.note: Liquid → gas gives the biggest increase in dispersal. Cooling and condensing decrease entropy.

items.topicLabel: R1.4 Entropy and spontaneity (additional higher level)
items.stem: A reaction is spontaneous at a given temperature when:
items.note: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS < 0 means the reaction is thermodynamically favourable. It may still be slow (kinetics).

items.topicLabel: R1.4 Entropy and spontaneity (additional higher level)
items.stem: Predict the sign of ΔS for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g).
choices: Positive, because a new compound is formed
Zero, because all species are gases
Negative, because the number of gas moles decreases from 4 to 2
Positive, because the reaction is exothermic
items.note: Fewer moles of gas → less dispersal → ΔS < 0. Count gas moles first.

items.topicLabel: R1.4 Entropy and spontaneity (additional higher level)
items.stem: Using S° values (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: N₂ 192, H₂ 131, NH₃ 193), ΔS° for N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ is:

items.topicLabel: R1.4 Entropy and spontaneity (additional higher level)
items.stem: A reaction has ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0. It is spontaneous:
items.note: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is negative only when TΔS > ΔH, i.e. at high T.

items.topicLabel: R1.4 Entropy and spontaneity (additional higher level)
items.stem: For a reaction with ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = −199 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, ΔG at 298 K is:

items.topicLabel: R1.4 Entropy and spontaneity (additional higher level)
items.stem: Above what temperature does the reaction in the previous question stop being spontaneous?
items.note: ΔG = 0 when T = ΔH/ΔS = 92 000 ÷ 199 = 462 K. Above this, the −TΔS term outweighs ΔH.

items.topicLabel: R1.4 Entropy and spontaneity (additional higher level)
items.stem: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g) has ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. The minimum temperature for decomposition is about:
items.note: T = ΔH ÷ ΔS = 178 000 ÷ 161 = 1106 K. Units: J with J.

items.topicLabel: R1.4 Entropy and spontaneity (additional higher level)
items.stem: ΔG° for a reaction is −17.1 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K. Which is correct about K?
choices: K is greater than 1, so products are favoured at equilibrium
K is less than 1, so reactants are favoured
K equals 1, so neither is favoured
K is negative because ΔG° is negative
items.note: ΔG° = −RT ln K. Negative ΔG° → ln K > 0 → K > 1 (here K ≈ 1000).

items.topicLabel: R1.4 Entropy and spontaneity (additional higher level)
items.stem: Which statement about ΔG and the position of equilibrium is correct?
choices: A negative ΔG° means the reaction goes to completion
ΔG° depends on how fast the reaction reaches equilibrium
At equilibrium ΔG = 0 for the reaction mixture
A positive ΔG° means no products form at all
items.note: ΔG of the mixture falls to zero at equilibrium. ΔG° only tells you where the equilibrium lies (K), never the rate.

items.topicLabel: R1.4 Entropy and spontaneity (additional higher level)
items.stem: Explain why the dissolving of ammonium nitrate in water is spontaneous even though it is endothermic.
markscheme: ΔS is positive: ions are released from the lattice and become dispersed in solution (1)
TΔS is larger than ΔH (at room temperature) (1)
So ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is negative (1)
items.tactic: Use the equation explicitly: state signs of ΔH and ΔS, then the sign of ΔG.

items.topicLabel: R1.4 Entropy and spontaneity (additional higher level)
items.stem: For the reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g), ΔH = −198 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = −188 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. (a) Calculate ΔG at 700 K. (b) Comment on spontaneity at this temperature and at higher temperatures.
markscheme: Above ~1053 K (ΔH/ΔS) ΔG becomes positive, so not spontaneous (1)
items.tactic: Always convert J to kJ before combining ΔH with TΔS.

items.topicLabel: R1.4 Entropy and spontaneity (additional higher level)
items.stem: Calculate the equilibrium constant K at 298 K for a reaction with ΔG° = −5.70 kJ mol⁻¹. (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
items.tactic: Use J, not kJ, in ΔG° = −RT ln K.

items.topicLabel: R1.4 Entropy and spontaneity (additional higher level)
items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) ΔG° for an invented reaction was measured at several temperatures: 300 K −20.0; 400 K −8.0; 500 K +4.0 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° is a straight line.
(a) Use the data to determine ΔS° (gradient). (b) Determine ΔH° (intercept at T = 0). (c) Find the temperature at which ΔG° = 0 and state what it means.
markscheme: (a) Gradient = (4.0 − (−20.0)) ÷ (500 − 300) = +0.120 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; ΔS° = −gradient = −120 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (1)
Above 467 K the reaction is no longer spontaneous / K < 1 (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
